div.p: PA PREFACE TO THE FIRST EDITION. SOME remarks on the text of the present edition of the Ion will be found under § 5 of the Introduction. To what is said there, it should be added that numerous established corrections of the MSS. have been adopted without remark, while more doubtful ones have been discussed as briefly as possible. A few original conjectures have been offered. In the lyric portions of the play the arrangement of the lines is that shown by Schmidt in his Monodien u. Wechselgesänge (Euripides), but the numbering of Dindorf's Poetae Scenici has been preserved. In the notes, though discussion has naturally been avoided for the most part, the rule has been occa- sionally relaxed. It is hoped that this will prove not to have been done without profit to the student. Masters who were at school when 'big' editions were of many authors the only ones to be procured, will remember that some of their most valuable lessons in scholarship were then, as later, derived

from discussions of moot points and the comparison of conflicting views, and will perhaps be disposed to agree that the 'cut and dried' style of annotation in school-books is at the present time in some danger of being carried to excess. Besides my obligations to previous editors, of which more particular acknowledgment will be found in the notes, I have to thank my friend Dr. Verrall for some valuable criticisms and suggestions. MALVERN COLLEGE, April 23, 1889. PREFACE TO THE SECOND EDITION. THE call for a second edition has afforded an oppor- tunity for correcting one or two blunders, and for modifying some of the views previously expressed. In accordance with a desire expressed by several critics and teachers, a complete scheme of the choric metres has been added, with necessary explanations. In Appendix D will be found a few additional notes taken from, or called for by, the publication of Dr. Verrall's edition of the play last year. The fact that my own original edition was stereotyped has prevented these being included in the body of the work. To Dr. Verrall's view of the play, evolved

with characteristic subtlety and maintained with his usual fearlessness, I will frankly say I am a convert (or pervert), and shall remain so until the position is proved untenable. At the same time no alteration has been made in the notes on this account. It remains to express my thanks to the writers of various friendly notices of the first edition, several of whose suggestions have been adopted. If I have not accepted all, I hope my failure to do so will be put down to stupidity, or any other amiable defect, rather than to self-will. In particular, it really dis- tresses me to say that I cannot give up my heresy (?) on the subject of Conditional and Indefinite Sen- tences, as briefly stated in some of the notes below, and set forth at length in the Classical Review, vol. 4, pp. 200 ff. Pressure of work has prevented my replying at length to what has been written against my contention, and this is not the place to reopen the discussion. In the meantime, however, I should take it as a favour if some orthodox grammarians will kindly send me translations in Latin and Greek of the following:- (Scene: Dover Pier.) "Porter, have you seen a very tall gentleman with a white hat? He is going up to London.' 'No, sir; but if he had a ticket for Victoria, he would be in the front part of the train; and if he had booked for Charing Cross, he would be behind." Translators will please

state what thought (if any) the porter suppresses with each protasis. As to 'Indefinite' sentences, a very distinguished Oxford scholar wrote to me “I cannot lay my finger on the crucial instance you re- quire [viz., a sentence like ὃs ἂν ᾅδῃ with the meaning 'whosoever is singing now'], but I should be sur- prised if I could not find it in Plato." Until such a sentence is produced from some classical author, I hope it will not be considered too presuming if I continue to maintain on this point the position of Athanasius contra mundum. CHRIST COLLEGE, BRECON, Oct. 9, 1891.

div.head: 1. The Story and the Play.
div.p: THE circumstances preceding the action of the play, as related in the prologue, are briefly as follows. Kreousa, daughter of Erechtheus King of Athens, secretly bears a child of which Apollo is the father. So soon as her babe is born, she places it in a cave under the cliffs of the Acropolis, whence Hermes, at his brother's request, removes the infant and places it, cradle and all, on the steps of Apollo's temple at Delphi. The priestess finds it there and causes it to be reared. In the meantime, Kreousa returning to the place where she had left her babe and not finding it, is tortured with doubt as to whether the child has been devoured by wild beasts and birds, or whether Apollo (as she had hoped he would do) has taken care of his offspring. Kreousa is subsequently given in marriage to Xouthos a prince of Achaia, but has no other children; and accordingly after some years Xouthos and his wife come to Delphi to consult the oracle on the subject of their continued childlessness.

ΕΥΡΙΠΙΔΟΥ ΙΩΝ. Its At this point the action of the play commences. progress will be found sketched in the notes intro- ductory to the several scenes. The story appears to have been altogether the poet's own invention; at least no traces of it are to be found elsewhere. It is evidently designed to flatter Athenian pride on a point on which they were peculiarly sensitive. The prevailing legends repre- sented the Ionian race (to which the Athenians belonged) as descended in part from a certain Xouthos, an alien and immigrant to Attic soil; but the poet will have none of this admixture of foreign blood. He boldly declares that while the eponymous Ion had for his mother one sprung from the literally auto- chthonous Erichthonios, his father was a god, and that god Apollo. We shall probably not be wrong if we suppose that Euripides found the immediate motive for his innovation in some contemporary occurrence which had accentuated the habitual mistrust and jealousy felt by Athenians towards the aliens settled among them. Some of the expressions of dislike to foreigners are very pointed, and look as though they had been intended to have some special significance for the audience. The play is one of the best and most pleasing that we have from the poet's pen. In the ingenuity of the plot and the skill with which it is developed, the 1 See at vv. 184, 237, 509, 725, 1106, 1250.

Ion perhaps stands before any other of Euripides' extant productions. The irony of the situations is throughout highly effective, and the interest roused at the very commencement of the action is never allowed to flag. The chief character, Ion, has been universally felt to be a highly beautiful and spiritual creation, and has even furnished a modern author with the whole motive for a tragedy bearing the same name.1 Kreousa, except when stung to revenge by the strongest provocation (as she fancies), is a gentle and loving woman whose fortunes we follow with concernment and sympathy. Indeed, the deep and genuine pathos with which the poet has sur- rounded her, first as injured maid, and then as sorrowing mother and insulted wife, forms the char- acteristic charm of the whole play. It is absolutely natural and true to life, and would alone justify Mrs. Browning's happy designation of the poet as 'Our Euripides the human.'" The date of the Ion and the trilogy to which it belonged are alike unknown. 'It can only be in- ferred, from the style of the versification, that it was intermediate between the earlier and severer com- positions, and the licentious and florid elegances of 1 Talfourd's Ion. The play has nothing else in common with that of Euripides. 2 See further at v. 859.

div.head: 2. Delphi and the Temple of Apollo.
div.p: ΕΥΡΙΠΙΔΟΥ ΙΩΝ. his later plays' (Paley). The commonly assigned date is accordingly about B.C. 425.1 'The situation of Delphi is one of the most striking and sublime in all Greece. It lies in the narrow vale of the Pleistus, which is shut in on one side by Mount Parnassus, and on the other by Mount Cirphis. At the foot of Parnassus is a lofty wall of rocks, called Phaedriades in antiquity, and rising 2000 feet above the level of the sea. This rocky barrier faces the south, and from its extremity two lower ridges descend towards the Pleistus. The rocky ground between these two ridges also slopes down towards the river, and in about the middle of the semicircular recess thus formed lay the town of Delphi, occupying the central area of a great natural theatre, to which its site is compared by the ancient writers. The northern barrier of the Phaedriades is cleft towards the middle into two stupendous cliffs, between which issues the far-famed Castalian spring, which flows down the hill into the Pleistus. The ancient town lay on both sides of the stream, but the greater part of it on the right or western bank, on which stands the 1 Euripides produced his first play, the Peliades, in B.С. 455, the year that Aeschylus died. He himself and Sophocles died в.с. 406.

modern village of Kastrí. Above the town was the sanctuary of the god, immediately under the Phae- driades.'¹ According to tradition five temples in succession occupied the site of the famous oracle. Three of these are altogether mythical. The first was said to have been made of laurel branches, the second of bees' wings, the third, which was the work of Hephaistos, of bronze. Of the fourth temple Pausanias says:-'Now the fourth temple was built by Trophonios and Agamedes, and tradition relates that it was made of stone. It was burnt down when Erxikleides was archon at Athens, in the first year of the 58th olympiad, when Diognetos of Kroton was victor' (548 B.C.). The story of its founding by the god upon his arrival at Krissa in search of a home is told in the Homeric Hymn to the Pythian Apollo, vv. 104 ff. :- 'And thou comest to Krissa, beneath snow-crown'd Parnassos, to the spur that lieth towards the west wind, and the cliff hangeth over above, and below runneth the deep rocky glen. And there the lord Phoibos Apollo determined to make him a beauteous 1 Dict. Geogr. s.v. Delphi. In the rest of this and the fol. lowing section I have also received considerable assistance from a recent article by Prof. Middleton in the Hellenic Journal, vol. 9. The chief ancient authorities are the traveller Pausanias (circ. A.D. 180) and Plutarch. b

ΕΥΡΙΠΙΔΟΥ ΙΩΝ. temple, and he spake a word :- "Here soothly I am minded to build a temple very fair, to be an oracle for men, who for ever shall gather to me here un- blemished hecatombs when they come to question me, both they that hold the rich Island of Pelops and the dwellers in Europe and the isles of the sea. And to them all then will I deliver unerring counsel, pro- nouncing oracles in my rich temple." So speaking, Phoibos Apollo laid down foundations broad and long throughout; and upon them Trophonios and Aga- medes, sons of Erginos, dear to the immortal gods, set a floor of stone. And thereabout countless tribes of men built the god a temple to dwell in of polished stones, to be famed in song for ever. And hard-by was the fair-flowing spring where the king, the son of Zeus, slew with a shaft from his strong bow a serpent huge and mighty, a fierce monster that wrought much hurt to men in the land, much hurt alike to them- selves and their long-striding sheep, for a bloody pest was she. And Phoibos Apollo vaunted over her, "There now rot (πύθεν) on the earth that feedeth men! Thou shalt not live to be an evil bane to mortals, who eating the fruit of the rich land shall gather here unblemished hecatombs." So spake he vaunting; and darkness shrouded her eyes, and the mighty strength of the sun rotted her there (κατέ- πυσε). And therefore now she is called Python ; and men call the king Apollo Pythian, because ..

the strength of the fierce sun rotted the monster on that spot.'¹ This is all we know of the building of the fourth temple. The Erginos mentioned above was a mythical king of Orchomenos and son of Poseidon. Trophonios himself had a temple and oracular cave at Lebadeia in Boeotia. The latter is the σηκός spoken of in v. 300 of this play. Like the ἄδυτον at Delphi it was subterranean. The fourth temple, Prof. Middleton remarks, must be the one referred to by Homer, Il. 9. 404- οὐδ᾽ ὅσα λάινος οὐδὸς ἀφήτορος ἐντὸς ἐέργει Φοίβου ᾿Απόλλωνος Πυθοῖ ἔνι πετρηέσσῃ.2 When this temple was destroyed it was decided by a decree of the Amphiktionic Council to build a new one on a scale of surpassing magnificence, at a total cost of 300 talents (about £72,000). The Delphians were to contribute a quarter of the sum, and the rest 1 The true origin of the name Πυθώ is unknown. The de- rivation from πυθέσθαι, to inquire, is no more likely than that from πύθεσθαι given above. The hymn goes on to describe how the god, needing priests for his temple, induced some sailors from Crete (cp. the adj. Κρής, Κρῆσσα, Cretan) to undertake the office. The purpose of this episode, like that of the Python, is purely etymological and intended to account for the people of Krissa (Κρίσσαιοι) being the original pos- sessors of the temple. * Πυθώ is the only name for the place known to Homer.

ΕΥΡΙΠΙΔΟΥ ΙΩΝ. was to be raised by voluntary contributions from the whole of the civilized world. The money was easily collected and the contract undertaken by some mem- bers of the Alkmaeonid family, at that time exiled from Athens. The architect was Spintharos, a Cor- inthian, of whom nothing more is known. The con tractors gained great praise for their liberality in the performance of the work; for whereas the contract specified only πώρινος λίθος ('the local lime-stone': Prof. Middleton), they employed for the front the more costly white marble from Paros. The style of the architecture was Doric, and its general design what is called hexastyle peri- pteral; i.e. the columns ran all round it and there were six at each end. It appears to have been finished, excepting perhaps the sculptures, by about 490 в.с. Pausanias describing the statues in the pediments (see at v. 188) says that the faces were partly done by the Athenian Praxias, a pupil of the famous Kalamis, and finished after his death by Androsthenes, also an Athenian. Pausanias does not mention the metopes, but that some of them at least were sculptured appears from this play (v. 190 ff.). 1 Mr. A. S. Murray has suggested that these sculptures belonged to an internal frieze. But how could they then have been visible to the audience? But for Prof. Middleton's statement that 'only those [metopes] within the Pro-naos appear to have been sculptured' (he gives no authority), it

On the architrave all round the temple were hung gilded bronze shields, half of them offered by the Athenians from the spoils taken at Marathon, the others given by the Aetolians in commemoration of their victory over the Gauls under Brennus in 279 B.C. The temple was entered through a Pro-naos or vestibule. In this Pausanias saw a bronze statue of Homer and the enormous silver crater (holding 600 amphorae) given by Croesus. The walls were inscribed with sayings of the Wise Men, such as γνῶθι σεαυτόν, μηδὲν ἄγαν, ἐγγύα· πάρα δ' ἄτα ('give surety, and thou'lt smart for it'). The famous E of Delphi also hung here. It was the mere letter carved in wood, and both its origin and meaning were a mystery even to the ancients. It was said to have been an offering of the Wise Men. From the Pro-naos we come to the body of the temple, the vaós or cella, where visitors consulting the oracle waited for their answers. It was hypaethral or open to the sky. Pausanias saw here an altar of Poseidon (see § 3), and statues of two of the Fates, in close proximity to which there stood one of Zeus Moirāgetes ('Leader of the Fates') occupying the place of the third Fate (ἀντὶ τῆς τρίτης). By the side of these stood a statue of Apollo, also in the would have been natural to suppose that the sculptures described in this play were on the outside of the eastern front of the temple.

ΕΥΡΙΠΙΔΟΥ ΙΩΝ. character of Moiragetes. The reason for the absence of the third Fate is not known. Here also was the ἑστία with its never-dying fire, by which the priest of Apollo slew Neoptolemos, and an iron chair in which Pindar used to sit whenever he visited the temple, singing such of his hymns as were written in honour of Apollo.¹ Close by the ἑστία stood the famous omphalos. It was a rounded conical white stone, similar in shape to half an egg, and of such a height that the suppliant could sit upon it. In works of art the omphalos is represented as flanked on either side by figures of the two eagles of the story,2 and as 1 Prof. Middleton places the ἑστία, Pindar's chair, and the omphalos, together with an elaborate iron crater-stand minutely described by Pausanias, all in the ἄδυτον. But if (as Prof. Middleton thinks, and the narrative certainly implies) Pau- sanias did not enter the ἄδυτον, how could he have seen these objects? That he did see them is evident from his language. In his plan Prof. Middleton places the crater-stand and Pindar's chair in the vaós (their natural place), and the ἑστία and ὀμφαλός in the ἄδυτον. But Pausanias expressly says that the chair is οὐ πόῤῥω τῆς ἑστίας, and mentions the ὀμφαλός immediately after the crater. 2 The story is that Zeus, wishing to discover the centre of the earth, dispatched two eagles, one from the east and one from the west, and that the omphalos at Delphi marks the point at which the birds met. The fact is that such stones were used in primitive ages as symbols of deity, and doubtless the one at Delphi was originally used for this purpose and was far more ancient than the worship of Apollo. See § 3.

covered with fillets (ταινίαι), which sometimes alter- nate with branches of bay. The fillets appear some- times hanging straight down the sides of the stone from the top, sometimes diagonally; sometimes they cross each other. The exact position of the ἑστία and ὀμφαλός remain uncertain. Dr. Smith (Dict. Geogr.) would place them as nearly as possible in the centre of the cella. The ἄδυτον was contained in the vaós and entered from it. Ancient writers in speaking of it use such words as ἄντρον, σπήλαιον, specus, cauerna; and as the priestess was said to descend into it, there is every reason to suppose that it was a subterraneous chamber below the level of the vaós (see on v. 220). Prof. Middleton thinks it was divided into two parts; one being the oracular vault or μαντεῖον proper, where the priestess sat upon the tripod, and the other a chamber immediately over this, on a level with the vaós, and communicating with the lower one by a hole in the floor through which the voice of the priestess was heard ἀείδουσ' "Ελλησι βοὰς, ἃς ἄν ᾿Απόλλων κελαδήσῃ (ν. 92). There was in the ἄδυτον a golden statue of Apollo, 'an altar with a fire of pine-wood on which the Pythia burnt bay-leaves and barley-meal 1 See several figures in Prof. Middleton's article, p. 295 ff. A marble copy of the omphalos was found at Athens a few years ago. It is truncated and now measures 2014 inches in height.

div.head: 3. The Oracle.
div.p: ΕΥΡΙΠΙΔΟΥ ΙΩΝ. (instead of fragrant incense) before descending to the oracular chasm," and some sacred armour. The rock which formed the bottom floor of the ἄδυτον was cleft by a fissure. The priestess was sup- ported over this by the tripod on which she sat, and was 'inspired' by certain gaseous exhalations which arose round her and produced the effect of delirium or intoxication. Delphi was an oracular centre long before the date of Apollo's worship, which was probably introduced there at the time of the founding of the fourth temple (see § 2). The legends name Poseidon and Earth as the first possessors of the oracle. According to Aeschylus (Eum. 2 ff.) the successors of Gaia were Themis and Phoibe, the latter of whom was the immediate predecessor of Apollo. All these older deities were χθόνιοι or powers of the lower world. They were not, however, entirely superseded by Apollo, for the worship of the chthonian Dionysos survived as a most important cult at Delphi and on Mount Parnassos, and he even shared Apollo's temple.2 At first oracles were given only once a year, but in historical times with much greater frequency. On 1 Prof. Middleton, from Plutarch. 2 See the description of the pediments, v. 188 1.

any day appointed for consultation of the god a general sacrifice for all comers was offered in front of the temple (cp. v. 419); if it proved favourable the day was αἰσία, and visitors drew lots for the order in which they should prefer their questions (cp. v. 422). The privilege of προμαντεία or precedence was occa- sionally granted to states and individuals. A person consulting the oracle offered a special victim for him- self and paid a fee. The management of the oracle as well as the government of the place was in the hands of certain 'nobles' of Delphi,¹ who performed their duties in an order determined by lot, as appears from ข. 416 of this play :- τῶν ἔσω δ᾽ ἄλλοις μέλει, οἱ πλησίον θάσσουσι τρίποδος, ὦ ξένε, Δελφῶν ἀριστῆς οὓς ἐκλήρωσεν πάλος. Five Delphian families traced their descent from Deukalion, and the heads of these enjoyed precedence over the other priests and were called "Όσιοι. These men seated in the adytum (see above, § 2) listened to the ravings of the Pythia and reduced them to intel- ligible form for the visitor, who awaited his answer in the vaós. In fact, it was they who really con- cocted the oracle. The answers were delivered 1 Called Δελφοὶ θέραπες, υ. 94; κοίρανοι Πυθικαί, υ. 1219 ; Δελφῶν ἄνακτες, υ. 1222; Πύθιοι, ν. 1251. They were also called προφῆται, interpretes : cp. v. 413 τίς προφητεύει θεοῦ;

ΕΥΡΙΠΙΔΟΥ ΙΩΝ. both verbally and in writing, at first in verse¹ and later in prose. Before taking her seat on the tripod the Pythia fasted for three days and bathed in the Kastalia. On the appointed day she first burnt bay-leaves and barley-meal on the ἑστία; she then descended into the vault, and having chewed some bay-leaves and drunk water from the sacred spring Kassotis, 2 mounted the tripod holding a branch of bay in her hand. In early times the priestess was a young maiden, but after- wards a change was made and no one was selected who was under fifty years of age. 'The Pythia was generally taken from some family of poor country people. At first there was only one Pythia at a time; but when Greece was in its most flourishing state, and when the number of those who came to consult the oracle was very great, there were always two Pythias, who took their seat on the tripod alter- nately, and a third was kept in readiness in case some accident should happen to either of the two others. The effect of the smoke on the whole mental and physical constitution is said to have some- times been so great that in her delirium she leaped from the tripod, was thrown into convul- 1Cp. v. 6 ὑμνῳδεῖ: v. 681 τίν'...ἔχρησας ὑμνῳδίαν ; 2 A small spring which disappeared in the ground near the temple.

div.head: 4. The Long Cliffs. The Cave of Pan. The Grotto of
div.p: sions, and after a few days died.' (Dict. Ant. s.v. oraculum.)¹ The πρόξενοι mentioned in v. 551 were a body of officials whose business it was to provide lodging and entertainment for the visitors, and generally to give them such information and assistance as they might desire with a view to consulting the oracle in proper form. This seems to have been part of Ion's duty. State embassies, or at least the most important of them, appear to have been entertained by the Delphians at the public expense. Besides that at Delphi there were twenty-one other oracles of Apollo in various parts of Hellas and Asia Minor. Aglauros. ... 'The rocks along the northern side of the Acropolis were called Long Rocks (Μακραί). This name is explained by the fact that the length of the Acropolis [from E. to W.) is much greater than its width; but it might have been given with equal propriety to the rocks on the southern side. The reason why the southern rocks had not the same name appears to have been that the rocks on the northern side could 1 The story is told by Plutarch of a Pythia who was forced to sit on the tripod against her will.

ΕΥΡΙΠΙΔΟΥ ΙΩΝ. be seen from the greater part of the Athenian plain, and from almost all the demi of Mt. Parnes; while those on the southern side were only visible from the small and more undulating district between Hymettus, the Long Walls, and the sea. In the city itself the rocks of the Acropolis were for the most part con- cealed from view by houses and public buildings.' .. 'The cave of Apollo and Pan, more usually called the cave of Pan, lay at the base of the N.W. angle of the Acropolis. It is described... by Pausanias as a little below the Propylaea, with a spring of water near it. The worship of Apollo in this cave was probably of great antiquity. The worship of Pan in this cave was not introduced till after the battle of Marathon, in consequence of the services which he rendered to the Athenians on that occasion. His statue was dedicated by Miltiades, and Simonides wrote the inscription for it. A statue of Pan, now in the public library at Cambridge, was discovered in a garden a little below the cave, and may possibly be the identical figure dedicated by Miltiades.' 'The sanctuary of Aglaurus, one of the three daughters of Cecrops, was also a cavern situated in the northern face of the Acropolis. It is evident from several passages in the Ion of Euripides that the Aglaurium was in some part of the precipices called the Long Rocks, which ran eastward of the grotto of Pan. It is said to have been the spot from

div.head: 5. The Text.
div.p: which Aglaurus and her sister Herse threw themselves from the rocks of the Acropolis upon opening the chest which contained Erichthonius; and it was also near this sanctuary that the Persians gained access to the Acropolis. At the distance of about 60 yards to the east of the cave of Pan and at the base of a precipice is a remarkable cavern; and 40 yards further in the same direction there is another cave much smaller, immediately under the wall of the citadel, and only a few yards distant from the northern portico of the Erechtheium. One of these two caves was undoubtedly the Aglaurium.' (Dict. Geogr. s.v. Athenae.) .. The Ion is found in two Mss. only of independent value: (1) the Palatine (P), now in the Vatican; (2) the Laurentian or Flor. 2 (C), now in the Laurentian Library at Florence. Both are of the fourteenth century. They are very incorrectly and ignorantly written copies made independently from the same original, and the archetype itself must have contained a number of serious errors. Various editors have corrected the orthographical blunders in each manu- script, and many certain conjectures have been made; but of C until a few years ago no trustworthy colla- tion had been made, and its true readings were in

ΕΥΡΙΠΙΔΟΥ ΙΩΝ. many places a matter of doubt.¹ In preparing the present edition I have had the advantage of the very careful examination of both Mss. by Möllendorf in 1875.2 In his judgment the value of the (original) readings of C is considerably higher than was formerly supposed. In a few unimportant instances where P and C were formerly supposed to differ I have silently followed Möllendorf in adopting a reading in which the two manuscripts have been found by him to agree. The following is a table of the passages in which new corrections have been offered. It will be observed that in almost every instance the MSS. are confessedly corrupt. 98 for ἀγαθόν 101 ἰδίας دو Πύθιος ἀγαθοί ἱλέας (Verrall.) δαίμων 286 τιμᾶ· τιμᾶ· ὡς τιμᾶ· τί μαίει ; وو دو دو دو دو دو دو προσήκει δ' τυραννίδος φίλα τύραννος ἡ φίλα φίλον 434 προσήκει τ' νοσῶ Νηρέος χορευόμεναι νοσεί Νηρηίδες κορευόμεναι (Musgr. & Ver.) 1 The same was true of the Palatine, but to a much smaller extent. 2 As published in his Analecta Euripidea. * The manuscript was freely 'corrected' (for the worse) by an ancient διορθωτής, and shows traces also of a third hand. div.head: 6. Structure of the Play.
div.p: 1093 for ἀθέμιτας 1099 ὁ Διὸς ἐκ 1106 κλειναί دو دو دو 1251 Πυθίω ἤ " 1489 δ' ἐμᾶς دو ἀθέμιτος ὧδε Διὸς εἶς (τε Διὸς εἶς, Ver.) κεδναί Πυθίων δέ μου 1. πρόλογος, υυ. 1–183. 2. πάροδος, νν. 184-236 (with κομμός, υν. 219-236). 3. ἐπεισόδιον πρῶτον, υν. 237-451. 4. στάσιμον πρῶτον, υυ. 452-508. 5. ἐπεισόδιον δεύτερον, υυ. 509-675. 6. στάσιμον δεύτερον, υυ. 676-724. 7. ἐπεισόδιον τρίτον, υυ. 725-1047 (with κομμός, υν. 747-807). 8. στάσιμον τρίτον, υυ. 1048–1105. 9. ἐπεισόδιον τέταρτον, νν. 1106-1128. 10. στάσιμον τέταρτον, νν. 1229-1249. 11. ἔξοδος, νν. 1250-1622.

ΕΥΡΙΠΙΔΟΥ ΙΩΝ. These parts of a tragedy are defined by Aristotle as follows (Poet. § 12) :- πρόλογος : μέρος ὅλον τραγῳδίας τὸ πρὸ χοροῦ παρόδου, all that precedes the entrance of the Chorus. πάροδος: ἡ πρώτη λέξις ὅλου χοροῦ, the first utterance of the whole Chorus (their 'entrance song'). ἐπεισόδιον : μέρος ὅλον τραγῳδίας τὸ μεταξὺ ὅλων χορικῶν μελῶν, all that stands between whole choric songs. στάσιμον : μέλος χοροῦ, τὸ ἄνευ ἀναπαίστου καὶ τροχαίου, a song of the Chorus employing neither anapaestic nor trochaic measures. (The name is in contrast to πάροδος, the στάσιμον being sung by the Chorus, when at their station in the ὀρχήστρα.) κομμός : θρήνος κοινὸς χοροῦ καὶ ἀπὸ σκηνής, α dirge in which the Chorus in the orchestra and the actors on the stage both bear part (contributing alter- nate portions). ἔξοδος : μέρος ὅλον τραγῳδίας μεθ' ὃ οὐκ ἔστι χοροῦ μέλος, all that follows the last song of the Chorus.
